title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F01
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 48 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

Summary of MOOC Content
Soil Moisture Dynamics
1. Importance of Soil Moisture:
   • Critical for vegetation growth, photosynthesis, soil temperature regulation, and microbial activity.
   • Controls the partitioning of solar radiation into sensible and latent heat fluxes and precipitation into infiltration and surface runoff.

2. Measurement Techniques:
   • Direct methods: Gravimetric sampling (drying soil samples).
   • Indirect methods: Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR) and radar remote sensing (e.g., L-band radar).

3. Key Concepts:
   • Dielectric constant: Water (~80) vs. dry soil (~2.6). Radar systems exploit this difference to estimate soil moisture.
   • Frequency dependence: Dielectric constant decreases with increasing frequency (relaxation frequency ~10 GHz).
   • Temperature dependence: Frozen soil immobilizes water molecules, making measurements impossible.

4. Remote Sensing Missions:
   • SMAP (NASA): L-band radiometer, 9–36 km resolution, 2–3 day revisit, ±0.04 volumetric soil moisture accuracy.
   • SMOS (ESA): L-band radiometer, 40 km resolution, 3-day revisit.
   • ASCAT (ESA): C-band scatterometer, 12.5–25 km resolution, daily observations.

5. Applications:
   • Drought monitoring, flood forecasting, irrigation optimization, and freeze-thaw cycle detection in Arctic regions.

Vegetation Water Stress
1. Key Concepts:
   • Soil moisture deficits directly impact vegetation health, photosynthesis, and crop yields.
   • Vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI, WDVI) are used to monitor vegetation health and water stress by correcting for soil background and atmospheric disturbances.

2. Biophysical Parameters:
   • Leaf Area Index (LAI): Quantifies the amount of green leaves per unit ground area.
   • Chlorophyll Content: Indicates plant health and photosynthetic capacity.
   • Canopy Chlorophyll Content (CCC): Product of LAI and leaf chlorophyll content.

3. Remote Sensing Techniques:
   • Sentinel-2: Used to derive vegetation indices (e.g., WDVI, CVI, CIGreen) for estimating LAI and chlorophyll content.
   • Temporal signatures: Track changes in reflectance over time to monitor crop growth and stress.

4. Key Regions and Examples:
   • Agricultural regions (e.g., U.S. Corn Belt): Soil moisture and vegetation health monitoring during growing seasons.
   • Arctic regions: Freeze-thaw cycle monitoring using radar remote sensing.

items.question: Find MOOC lectures about radar-based ocean remote sensing, including how SAR is used to detect oil spills and measure sea surface wind and waves.

answers.text:
Here are the relevant MOOC lecture transcripts addressing radar-based ocean remote sensing, specifically SAR for oil spill detection and sea surface wind and wave measurement:

1. SAR for Oil Spill Detection
From: Sea Ice - Operational use of SAR at Canadian Ice Service
The additional benefit of all this monitoring is that SAR can be used to identify and track potential oil pollution in the world's oceans. When there is an oil spill in the ocean, the area with the floating oil looks very different from the surrounding waters without any pollution because the oil suppresses the small capillary waves. On SAR imagery, these areas of oil pollution look darker because they reflect less radar energy than the unpolluted water surface around them. This type of monitoring can be carried out during any time of day or night, and in cloudy or foggy conditions.

2. SAR for Sea Surface Wind and Wave Measurement
From: ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Sea Surface Wind
The synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has a fantastic capability to detect surface roughness at the ocean surface with very high spatial resolution. This allows us to extract information about sea surface wind, which is a dominant contributor to surface roughness. Wind at the ocean surface has two properties: speed and direction, and SAR can detect both in a single image.

• Wind Direction: If the wind blows toward the radar antenna, it produces a strong return signal. If it blows across the radar look direction, the sensitivity is weaker. This directional sensitivity is both valuable and challenging. Near land, wind direction can be inferred from the signal in coastal areas, while in the open ocean, large-scale weather conditions are often used to estimate direction.
• Wind Speed: SAR can detect wind speeds ranging from a few meters per second up to hurricane-force winds (above 30 m/s). The spatial resolution of SAR (hundreds of meters) allows for detailed observations of low-pressure systems, which are not possible with traditional observing systems.

SAR is also used to study ocean waves. Waves have characteristic wavelengths (typically hundreds of meters) and patterns that are easily detectable in SAR imagery due to its fine spatial resolution. SAR can characterize:
• Wavelength: The distance between wave crests.
• Amplitude: The height of the waves.
• Wave Spectrum: Used in ocean wave modeling to predict changes in wave patterns over time.

SAR observations are combined with wave models to improve forecasts of ocean surface roughness. For example, waves generated by low-pressure systems in the southern hemisphere can travel across the Pacific Ocean, cross the equator, and reach the shores of Alaska in 10–15 days. SAR data allows us to monitor these long-distance wave patterns.

From: ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Bragg Scattering
The most common wavelength used in SAR is C-band (around 6 cm). When this electromagnetic wave interacts with the ocean surface, Bragg scattering occurs, where small capillary waves (with wavelengths comparable to the radar wavelength) dominate the backscatter. This principle is fundamental for detecting sea surface roughness, wind, and waves using SAR.

The MOOC transcripts provide the following information on radar-based ocean remote sensing:

• Sea Surface Wind and Waves:
    • Wind: SAR detects surface roughness with high spatial resolution, allowing for the measurement of both wind speed (from a few m/s up to hurricane speeds over 30 m/s) and wind direction. Higher wind speeds increase surface roughness, leading to increased radar backscatter and brighter image tones.
    • Waves: SAR can detect ocean surface wave patterns (typically around 100 meters in wavelength). By characterizing the wavelength and amplitude, the wave spectrum can be estimated for ocean wave modeling. This is often linked to Bragg scattering, where C-band radar interacts with small capillary waves that are modulated by longer ocean waves.

• Oil Spill Detection:
    • SAR is used to identify and track oil pollution because floating oil suppresses small capillary waves. This makes oil spills appear as darker areas on SAR imagery compared to the surrounding unpolluted water, as they reflect less radar energy.

Relevant Lectures:
• ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Sea Surface Wind
• Sea Ice - Operational use of SAR at Canadian Ice Service
• ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Bragg Scattering

[1] ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Sea Surface Wind
Key Topics: SAR for ocean surface wind measurement, wave detection, and surface current analysis.

Excerpt:
The synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has a unique capability to detect surface roughness at the ocean surface with very high spatial resolution. This allows us to isolate the contribution of surface wind to roughness, as wind speed and direction significantly influence radar backscatter. SAR can detect wind speeds ranging from a few meters per second to hurricane-force winds (over 30 m/s) with spatial resolutions of hundreds of meters, revealing fine details of low-pressure systems.

For wave observation, SAR detects patterns of ocean surface waves with wavelengths typically in the order of hundreds of meters. By analyzing these patterns, we can characterize wave amplitude and wavelength, estimate wave spectra, and improve ocean wave forecasting models. SAR data has even captured waves generated in the Southern Hemisphere crossing the Pacific Ocean and reaching the shores of Alaska.

After accounting for wind and wave contributions to surface roughness, the remaining signal can be attributed to surface currents. SAR can detect surface current boundaries, which are crucial for understanding vertical motions and biological activity. Recent advancements allow direct retrieval of surface velocity using the Doppler principle, where phase shifts in SAR signals reveal the motion of the ocean surface. By isolating wind and wave contributions, the residual phase shift provides insights into surface currents.

[2] Sea Ice - Operational Use of SAR at Canadian Ice Service
Key Topics: SAR for oil spill detection, wind field analysis, and ice monitoring.

Excerpt:
SAR is extensively used by the Canadian Ice Service for monitoring sea ice, glacial ice, and lake ice, which are critical for safe navigation. SAR imagery is analyzed in near real-time to produce ice charts that support maritime operations, including those of the Canadian Coast Guard and shipping companies.

One of the key applications of SAR is the detection of oil spills. When oil is present on the ocean surface, it suppresses small capillary waves, resulting in darker areas on SAR images due to reduced radar backscatter. This allows for effective monitoring of oil pollution during day, night, and in cloudy or foggy conditions.

SAR images also reveal the impact of near-surface wind fields on ocean surface roughness. Higher wind speeds increase surface roughness, leading to brighter image tones due to increased radar backscatter. This relationship enables the derivation of wind information from SAR data, making it a valuable tool for oceanographic and meteorological applications.

These excerpts provide detailed insights into how SAR is used for ocean remote sensing, including the detection of oil spills, measurement of sea surface wind, and analysis of ocean waves and currents.

items.question: Search MOOC content about extreme precipitation events and disaster risk reduction. Based on a major flood case study discussed in the content, download hourly ERA5 precipitation for the affected region and period and aggregate to daily sums.

answers.text:
The MOOC content identifies a major flood case study in Iran (2019), where severe flash flooding occurred between mid-March and April 2019, particularly affecting provinces like Kurdistan, Fars, Khuzestan, and Lorestan, as well as the city of Akala in Golestan.

I have successfully downloaded the hourly ERA5 total precipitation data for the affected region and period:
• March 2019: precip_iran_2019_03.nc
• April 1st to 14th, 2019: precip_iran_2019_04.nc

Regarding the aggregation to daily sums, the GIS analysis server is optimized for spatial operations on GeoTIFFs and vectors rather than temporal resampling of NetCDF files. To complete this step, the standard procedure is to use the xarray library in Python to resample the tp variable to daily sums (.resample(time='D').sum()).

The MOOC content highlights the severe flash flooding event in Iran in 2019 as a major case study for extreme precipitation and disaster risk reduction. The event affected millions, displaced thousands, and caused significant economic losses, particularly in agricultural areas. The floods were driven by three major rainfall waves between mid-March and mid-April 2019, with extreme precipitation events (e.g., March 17th, where rainfall exceeded 70% of the annual average in hours).

ERA5 Precipitation Data for Iran (March 15 – April 14, 2019)
Hourly ERA5 precipitation data for the affected region (bounding box: [25.0, 44.0, 39.0, 63.0]) has been downloaded and split into two files:
1. era5_precip_hourly_2019_03_15_31_full.nc
2. era5_precip_hourly_2019_04_01_14_full.nc

Next Steps for Aggregation
To aggregate the hourly data to daily sums, you can use the following approaches locally:

Option 1: Using Python (xarray)

import xarray as xr

Load the datasets
ds1 = xr.open_dataset("era5_precip_hourly_2019_03_15_31_full.nc")
ds2 = xr.open_dataset("era5_precip_hourly_2019_04_01_14_full.nc")

Combine the datasets
combined = xr.concat([ds1, ds2], dim="valid_time")

Aggregate to daily sums
daily_sum = combined["tp"].resample(valid_time="1D").sum()

Save the result
daily_sum.to_netcdf("era5_precip_daily_2019_03-15_04-14.nc")

Option 2: Using CDO (Climate Data Operators)

cdo daysum era5_precip_hourly_2019_03_15_31_full.nc era5_precip_hourly_2019_04_01_14_full.nc era5_precip_daily_2019_03-15_04-14.nc

Here is what the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy says about monitoring forests and deforestation from space, along with a matching MOOC lecture on the same topic:

ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy: Forests and Deforestation Monitoring
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy highlights the critical role of satellite-based monitoring in addressing Science Questions (SQs) related to forests and deforestation, including:

1. Global Carbon Cycle (SQ-01)
   • Forests act as key carbon sinks, and deforestation significantly impacts carbon cycles.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Quantify CO₂ and CH₄ emissions and removals.
     • Distinguish anthropogenic vs. natural emissions.
     • Quantify fluxes from managed lands.
   • Tipping Points: Directly linked to TP-05 (Tropical Forests), TP-06 (Boreal Forests), and TP-07 (Temperate Forests).

2. Land Biosphere Responses (SQ-02)
   • Focuses on how the land biosphere responds to human activity and climate change.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Quantify land source/sink distribution and drivers.
     • Quantify roles of climate and disturbances on the land carbon sink.
     • Quantify above-ground biomass in forests.
     • Catalogue climate impacts on crop health and forest mortality.

3. State of Land Ecosystems (SQ-55)
   • Improves ecosystem characterization by structure, composition, and functions worldwide.

4. Ecosystems Transitions (SQ-56)
   • Investigates where and how ecosystems are undergoing critical transitions.

Strategic Objectives Supporting Forest Monitoring
• SO-02: Advance Earth science understanding within key themes, including Ecosystem Health (ST-IV).
• SO-05: Maximize mission exploitation (2026–2031) to advance forest monitoring.
• SO-10: Foster collaboration through ESA Science Clusters and the Earth System Science Hub.
• SO-14: Promote open science and digital innovation, including AI/ML for analyzing EO data related to forests.

Key Missions and Data Sources
• Landsat: Optical and thermal data for vegetation dynamics.
• Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2: SAR and optical data for forest structure and composition.
• Radar Sensors: C-band (e.g., Sentinel-1) and L-band (e.g., future missions) for biomass and deforestation monitoring.

Matching MOOC Lecture
[1] ESA Echoes in Space - Land: Introduction to Forest Monitoring
This lecture covers:
• The role of radar sensors (C-band and L-band) in monitoring forests and deforestation.
• How radar can measure forest biomass, canopy height, and subtle changes like degradation or regrowth.
• The importance of forests in terrestrial carbon dynamics and climate change models.
• The use of time series and interferometry to differentiate forests from other land cover types.
• Applications in policies like Reduced Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation (REDD+).

Would you like to explore specific missions, datasets, or additional MOOC resources on this topic?

Here are the results for your request:

ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy on Monitoring Forests and Deforestation from Space
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy highlights the importance of satellite-based monitoring for forests and deforestation, aligning with global initiatives like the UN SDGs, Paris Agreement, and UN CBD. Key objectives include:
• Climate change mitigation by monitoring forests as carbon sinks/sources.
• Biodiversity conservation through deforestation and degradation tracking.
• Sustainable development via data-driven policy support.
• Early warning systems for illegal logging and forest fires.

Technologies and Methods:
• Optical Remote Sensing (Sentinel-2, Landsat): High-resolution imagery for forest cover, health, and change detection (e.g., NDVI, EVI). Limited by cloud cover.
• Radar Remote Sensing (Sentinel-1, ALOS-2): Cloud-penetrating, day/night operation for forest structure, biomass, and degradation detection (InSAR, PolInSAR).
• LiDAR (ICESat-2, GEDI): 3D forest structure and biomass estimation.
• Time-Series Analysis: Dense data from Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat for detecting deforestation, degradation, and regrowth (e.g., BFAST, CCDC).
• Data Fusion: Combining optical, radar, and LiDAR for improved accuracy.
• AI/ML: Automating deforestation detection and land-cover classification.

Applications:
• Tropical deforestation (Amazon, Congo Basin) for conservation and policy enforcement.
• Boreal/temperate forests for fire, pest, and climate impact assessment.
• Carbon accounting for REDD+ and greenhouse gas inventories.
• Disaster response for wildfires and storms.

Challenges: Data gaps, cloud cover, and integrating multi-source data for higher accuracy.

   Summary:
   • Covers global forest loss drivers (logging, agriculture, mining) and their environmental/economic impacts.
   • Demonstrates Sentinel-2 time-series for deforestation/regrowth detection and Sentinel-1 radar for near-real-time logging alerts.
   • Focuses on time-series analysis and near-real-time applications for law enforcement (e.g., illegal logging in Brazil).

2. Lecture: Introduction to Forest Monitoring
   Module: ESA Echoes in Space - Land (ESA MOOC)
   Summary:
   • Explores radar remote sensing (C-band, L-band) for biomass estimation and carbon storage.
   • Highlights REDD+ and climate modeling applications.
   • Discusses radar interferometry for forest height and structure, with examples from Copernicus Sentinel satellites.

3. Lecture: Time Series Methods for Forest Monitoring
   Module: Forest Monitoring (Wageningen University)
   Summary:
   • Compares time-series analysis (e.g., BFAST, CCDC) with bi-temporal methods for detecting deforestation timing and regrowth.
   • Integrates optical and radar data (Sentinel-1/2) for cloud-resistant monitoring.
   • Case studies: Deforestation in Guyana and near-real-time alerts for selective logging in Bolivia.

The MODIS Land Surface Temperature dataset provides daytime and nighttime land surface temperature at 1 km spatial resolution. The data can be filtered for specific time periods or locations, and the values are converted from Kelvin to Celsius for analysis. The dataset includes properties such as observation time, which is crucial for time-series analysis. Visualization tools allow for the inspection of temperature patterns, such as differences between urban and green areas."

These excerpts provide detailed explanations of how MODIS measures land surface temperature, including data resolution, temporal coverage, and practical applications in environmental monitoring.

Here are the most relevant MOOC lecture segments explaining how satellite sensors like MODIS measure land surface temperature (LST) for environmental monitoring:

[Urban Land Cover Mapping: Lecture about Urban Monitoring with MODIS Data based LST]
• MODIS Land Surface Temperature (LST) Dataset:
  • Provides global daytime and nighttime LST at 1 km spatial resolution.
  • Available as daily observations or composite products (e.g., 8-day or monthly averages).
  • Used for time-series analysis in environmental monitoring, such as tracking urban heat islands or climate trends.

[Urban Land Cover Mapping: Urban Monitoring LST with MODIS Data]
• Data Processing Workflow:
  1. Loading the Dataset:
     • MODIS LST data is accessed as an image collection (a stack of homogeneous rasters) in tools like Google Earth Engine.
  2. Temporal Filtering:
     • Data can be filtered by date ranges (e.g., specific months or seasons) to focus on relevant periods.
  3. Unit Conversion:
     • MODIS LST data is originally provided in Kelvin with a scaling factor (e.g., 0.02).
     • Conversion to Celsius requires:
       • Multiplying by the scaling factor (e.g., LST_Kelvin = LST * 0.02).
       • Subtracting 273.15 to convert Kelvin to Celsius (LST_Celsius = LST_Kelvin - 273.15).
  4. Visualization:
     • LST data can be visualized using statistical reducers (e.g., mean, max, min) to analyze spatial patterns.
     • Example: Mapping daytime LST with a color gradient (e.g., green to red) to highlight temperature variations.

[Sensor Accuracy: Introduction to Accuracy in Remote Sensing]
• Measurement Challenges:
  • Electromagnetic radiation is a challenging parameter to measure precisely due to:
    • Atmospheric interference (e.g., clouds, aerosols).
    • Sensor distance (satellites orbiting hundreds of kilometers above Earth).
  • Vicarious Validation:
    • Ground-based measurements are used to validate satellite radiance data.
    • Large, homogeneous areas (e.g., deserts or water bodies) are monitored simultaneously by satellites and ground instruments to ensure accuracy.
  • Atmospheric Correction:
    • Converts top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance to surface reflectance (bottom-of-atmosphere).
    • Essential for deriving land surface temperature and other surface properties.

How MODIS Measures LST
1. Thermal Infrared (TIR) Sensors:
   • MODIS uses thermal infrared bands (e.g., bands 31 and 32, centered at ~11 and 12 µm) to detect emitted thermal radiation from the Earth's surface.
   • The split-window algorithm (using two TIR bands) corrects for atmospheric effects (e.g., water vapor absorption).
2. Brightness Temperature:
   • The sensor measures radiance in the TIR bands, which is converted to brightness temperature (a proxy for surface temperature).
3. Atmospheric Correction:
   • Algorithms account for atmospheric absorption and emission to derive land surface temperature.
4. Validation:
   • Ground-based measurements (e.g., from weather stations or field campaigns) are used to validate MODIS LST products.
